title: Everyday Design Knowledge: A Knowledge-in-Pieces Perspective on HCI Learning
abstract: Learning sciences research shows that intuitive physics knowledge productively supports disciplinary learning through the Knowledge in Pieces (KiP) framework, which treats learners’ everyday intuitions as productive resources. We argue that similar parallels exist in HCI education, where students’ intuitive design knowledge can ground the development of interaction design expertise. Students live in a world saturated with professionally designed artifacts and routinely engage in “everyday design”, cultivating tacit knowledge about interfaces long before formal HCI instruction. This mirrors how intuitive physics knowledge develops through daily physical experience. To support this argument, we analyze first-week assignment submissions from an introductory HCI course in which students critiqued interactive systems. Our findings show that students enter HCI instruction with rich, nuanced intuitions about interface evaluation. We therefore suggest that (1) students’ prior intuitive knowledge is a valuable pedagogical resource for HCI educators, and (2) operationalizing a KiP approach can advance future HCI education research.

Challenge of Developing Expertise Following Faiola’s call to center design methodologies in the HCI curriculum, interaction design has become a mainstay of the modern HCI classroom [5, 32]. In higher education computing and engineering programs, these courses now serve the dual purpose of introducing future software developers to human-centered design principles while simultaneously providing an entry point for students explicitly pursuing careers as design professionals in industry (e.g. as UX designers or product designers) [20, 31]. To facilitate these aims, educators have increasingly moved beyond traditional lecture-based formats, adopting pedagogical models from design disciplines like studio-based and project-based learning which foster authentic, constructivist learning environments that mirror professional practice [9, 32]. By immersing students in iterative cycles of research, ideation, and critique, these courses aim to expand students’ value systems beyond functionality, transforming technical problem-solvers into designers capable of creating technologies that are effective and inclusive for diverse end-users.

[10] note a persistent difficulty in shifting focus from functionality to usability, observing that students often struggle to decouple the “correctness” of their implementation from the quality of the interaction. Collectively, these studies frame novice behaviors as practical barriers that need to be overcome to successfully adopt a design mindset and develop design expertise. These practical difficulties are frequently attributed to a deeper “cultural clash” between the epistemological traditions of engineering and design [19]. Gray et al. [9] argue that computing students often exhibit a form of “scientism”, approaching problems with an expectation of verifiable, binary correctness that is fundamentally at odds with the pluralistic nature of design. As such, the design studio’s emphasis on messy, iterative exploration is often at odds with the efficiency-oriented values present in computer science and

engineering curricula [19]. Consequently, students may resist the ambiguity in “wicked” problems, viewing the lack of a single optimal solution as a flaw in the pedagogical structure, rather than as a feature of the design space. This misalignment often leads students to treat formative activities inherent to the design studio, such as critique and feedback sessions, as “subjective grading mechanisms” rather than learning dialogues, as they struggle to reconcile the open-ended nature of design inquiry with their prior experience in more objective, metric-based assessment [13]. To address these initial struggles and the desired design expertise, HCI pedagogy identifies certain catalytic instructional activities designed to challenge students’ preconceptions about design. Zoltowski et al. [33] describe these as “critical experiences” or “wake-up calls” like when a technically sound design fails to resonate with users, forcing a re-evaluation of priorities.

By investigating the underlying mechanisms of change, researchers aim to facilitate the path from naive understanding to disciplinary expertise - an endeavor which ultimately engages with deep theoretical issues regarding what knowledge is, why it is difficult to acquire, and how a learner’s prior conceptual ecology organizes and constrains future learning [15, 34]. The Knowledge-in-Pieces (KiP) framework models knowledge as an ecology or a system of quasi-independent, small-grained knowledge elements that are contextually cued and activated. In KiP, learning is viewed as an “evolutionary” reorganization and refinement of these elements and activation heuristics into larger, more stable cognitive systems. Rather than treating prior knowledge as errors or misconceptions, KiP views these elements as productive resources that must be realigned into coherent knowledge structures to function within expert contexts.

Operationalizing KiP in HCI In this work, we propose that a KiP approach would be productive in analyzing how students develop design expertise in the modern HCI classroom. We do this because KiP models knowledge as a complex system consisting of many interacting parts rather than a single unified mental model - a view we find consistent with the pluralistic nature of design practice. Furthermore, the framework’s evolutionary perspective on learning which asserts that students possess rich conceptual resources rather than simply “wrong” or “unproductive” ideas, allows us to fundamentally reframe the starting point of the HCI learner. Just as physics students enter the classroom with a wealth of “intuitive physics” derived from their physical interactions with the world, computing and engineering students enter the HCI classroom with a vast reservoir of everyday design knowledge cultivated through their years of experience with designed digital artifacts.

They have tacitly learned rules about how interfaces work, how systems respond, and what constitutes a “good” interaction, all of which serve as the raw material for developing disciplinary design expertise. Conceptually, our work contributes a theoretical framework that reframes the HCI learner. By mapping the general structures of KiP onto the domain of interaction design, we provide a vocabulary to describe student reasoning as a complex system built on top of everyday design knowledge and existing epistemological resources. Our empirical contribution with this work can therefore be seen as a “proof of existence”, of sorts. To validate this theoretical reframing, we see it as appropriate to demonstrate that students do indeed possess these productive resources before formal instruction takes hold. If the KiP hypothesis holds for HCI, then student’s critiques should reveal more than just “misconceptions” or “fixations”, instead showcasing a rich logic derived from everyday interactions with digital interfaces.

This study operationalizes this inquiry by analyzing first-week critiques, seeing as they represent a moment where students are forced to articulate their design judgement and intuition [30] for evaluating interfaces before they have mastered the disciplinary vocabulary. We are therefore not looking for instances of expert performance but rather for seeds of expertise in the form of intuitive resources that students operationalize (i.e. cue and activate) when asked to evaluate the designed world around them.

A KiP approach suggests an alternative framing and tells us that expertise involves not just possessing the right knowledge elements, but knowing when to activate them. Rather than viewing student behaviors as deficits to be corrected, we might view them as context-dependent activations of cognitive resources. A learner who “rushes” to implementation may be activating a resource for verification, a behavior that is productive and rewarded in software engineering contexts but less appropriate during early design explorations. A learner who is “STUCK” or fixating on familiar UI patterns may be activating a pattern-matching resource that serves them well in debugging or algorithm design, but constraints design ideation. From this perspective, the documented struggles of computing students in the design studio are not character flaws or failures of understanding.

While design and engineering disciplines have deep rooted traditions, framing this as a cultural clash is unproductive and hides the continuity between student intuition and design expertise. The efficiency intuitions, pattern-recognition skills, and systematic thinking that engineering students bring are not antithetical to design, they are valuable resources that designers also employ. A KiP lens helps students expand and refine the contexts in which they activate different resources.

Each of the design primitives we identified is productive in some contexts but may lead to unproductive judgements in others. Instruction can help students develop more refined activation conditions. Here are a few examples: • Effort-Outcome Proportionality: Students readily detect unnecessary friction, but may over-apply this intuition to contexts where friction is intentional. Instruction can introduce cases of deliberate friction, e.g. confirmation dialogs before irreversible actions, speed bumps that encourage reflection, authentication steps for security etc. and help students reframe the question from "Is there friction?" to "Is this friction serving a purpose?" • Directness and Visibility: Students expect important features to be immediately visible, but may critique progressive disclosure as "hiding" functionality.

As we conclude, we reflect on the broader implications of this shift for the future of HCI education research, emphasizing that we need to continue mapping these intuitive resources and understanding how they evolve into professional expertise.

Expanding this line of research to more diverse student populations could reveal how different cultural and digital experiences shape the repertoire of everyday design knowledge that learners bring to the classroom. Ultimately, this Knowledge-in-Pieces approach offers HCI education researchers a new theoretical lens through which to examine the development of disciplinary expertise and HCI educators a new vocabulary for their work. Adopting a resource-based perspective offers a path toward more inclusive and effective HCI pedagogy. Recognizing the continuity between everyday design knowledge and disciplinary expertise may help alleviate the friction students experience in an HCI design studio. Formal concepts become extensions of existing intuitions, and the goal of HCI education moves towards helping learners coordinate and cue their existing resources towards expert-like design practice.

title: Investigating Instructional Design Expertise: A 25-Year Review of Literature
abstract: Defining instructional design expertise has been a concern among scholars for many years. Understanding expertise and expert performance is complex due to the nature of ill-structured problems and the variety of contexts in which instructional designers work. If the field seeks to effectively prepare designers and enhance performance in existing professionals, a unified understanding and definition of expertise is needed. This 25-year review evaluated existing definitions in well-established literature. Findings revealed a lack of a clear, consistently used definition. Scholars predominately used expert characteristics to conceptualize expertise. A synthesis of these characteristics illuminated three traits of expert instructional designers: knowledge, skills, and dispositions. These traits informed the creation of a new definition. Innovations in research, theory, and practice are discussed which would provide new avenues for understanding, developing, and evaluating expertise over the next 25 years. © 2021 International Society for Performance Improvement.

“The study of expertise seeks to understand and account for what distinguishes outstanding individuals in that domain from less outstanding individuals” (Ericsson & Smith, 1991, p. 2). U nderstanding the characteristics of expert instructional designers has been a goal for many years. In the early 1980s, scholars explored problem solving and design decision mak - ing, however, expertise was not explicitly mentioned (Kerr, 1983; Silber, 1981). Beginning in the 1990s, the terms expertise and instructional design expertise (IDE) emerged (LeMaistre, 1998; Perez, Johnson, & Emery, 1995; Rowland, 1992). During this time, LeMaistre (1998) cited, “there appears to be no definition of the expert instructional designer, nor of what consti - tutes expert practice in any component of instructional design” (p. 21). In the mid-1990s, researchers compared expert and novice characteristics, including design thinking (Perez et al., 1995; Perez & Emery, 1995).

Moving into the 2000s, scholars focused on experts’ design processes, including how they solved complex problems (Ertmer & Stepich, 2005; Ertmer et al., 2008, 2009a; Ertmer, York, & Gedik, 2009b; Kirschner, Carr, van Merrienboer, & Sloep, 2002). Over the past decade, Delphi studies have identified distinguishing characteristics of expert designers including leadership and the use of common principles (e.g., rules, heuristics) to guide their practice (Ashbaugh, 2013; York & Ertmer, 2011, 2016). Foundational expertise researchers have provided insight into experts’ thinking, problem-solving, and instructional design practice identifying Defining instructional design expertise has been a concern among scholars for many years. Understanding expertise and expert performance is complex due to the nature of ill-structured problems and the variety of contexts in which instructional designers work.

Articles which contained the terms instructional design/designer and expertise, experienced, or expert in the title, abstract, or key words were included. Related key words such as coached expertise, coaching instructional design novices, and instructional design competence were also included. Discussions of expertise in other disciplines, including teachers, were eliminated. (b) Were articles published in peer-reviewed journals between 1992–2017? Dissertations, conference proceedings, or other unpublished works were not included. Third, I retrieved and read 22 articles. For example, “expertise is manifested in a designer’s ability to produce meaningful problem representations by integrating information in a given situation with [their] prior knowledge and experience” (Ertmer et al., 2008; Ertmer et al., 2009a, p. 117; Rowland, 1992). One definition of an ID expert was “a solver of ill-defined problems” (Ertmer et al., 2008, p. 117). Expertise was also conceptualized by describing expert designers’ thinking, design process, and design products (Ertmer & Stepich, 2005; Hardre et al., 2005). For example, designers who think like an expert “will naturally begin to engage in the reflective, adaptive practices of the expert, and create the carefully considered products of the expert” (Ertmer & Stepich, 2005, p. 38; Hardre et al., 2005). (1995) 5 4 Rowley (2005) 2 York and Ertmer (2011) 2 York and Ertmer (2016) 4 Expert Characteristics In this review, expert characteristics primarily “[constitute] instruc - tional design expertise” (Perez et al., 1995, p. 344). The above defini - tions highlight aspects of experts’ knowledge (e.g., complex, integrated thinking), skills (e.g., problem-solving, strategic planning), dispositions (e.g., adaptive, reflective), and practice or performance (e.g., appropriate selection of design strategies, context-sensitive solutions). All articles in this review addressed aspects of ID knowledge and skill. Dispositions were also mentioned by a majority of authors (11/14), and half of the articles evaluate differences between expert and novice performance.

Taking an in-depth look at scholarship over the past 25 years has identified knowledge, skills, and dispositions as traits of expert instruc - tional designers. Across a variety of disciplines, knowledge and skills are cited as distinguishing characteristics of experts and identified in definitions and theories as primary components of expertise (Bransford, Brown, & Cocking, 2000; Chase & Simon, 1973; De Groot, 1965; Drey - fus & Dreyfus, 1986; Germain & Ruiz, 2008; Glasser & Chi, 1988; Her - ling, 2000; Kuchinke, 1997). In light of existing expertise research, ID knowledge and skills are not surprising findings but represent important components to consider when defining IDE. A unique contribution of this review identifies ID dispositions (e.g., adaptability, flexibility) as a trait of expert designers. Dispositions have not been explicitly considered in general expertise research, but the idea parallels the concept of adaptive expertise.

The International Board of Standards for Training, Performance, and Instruction (IBSTPI) defines IDE as “the level of knowledge and experience demonstrated by design - ers who are typically categorized as either novice, experienced, or expert” (Ritchey, Fields, & Foxon, 2000, p.181). This definition cites knowledge as a component of expertise but does not mention skills or dispositions. Categorizing designers (e.g., novice, experienced, expert) is needed for research and measurement purposes but does not conceptually provide an understanding of what expertise is. The IBSTPI definition of an expert instructional designer provides more insight and includes “the facility to anticipate design problems quickly and identify effective design solutions” (p. 146). This definition captures aspects relating to skills and superior performance but does not include knowledge in conjunction with these abilities.

Expertise theory focused on understanding individual processes, including the role dis - positions may play in producing quality products and solutions is also needed. Differentiating instructional, instructional design, and instruc - tional design expertise theory would be a worthy goal for theorists. Practice Scholars have considered how expertise develops for many years (Ertmer & Stepich, 2005; Ge & Hardre, 2010; Stepich, Ertmer, & Lane, 2001; Verstegen, Barnard, & Pilot, 2008). Re-defining expertise has implications for informing training practices. First, novice design - ers need to gain foundational knowledge, including ID models and theories (York & Ertmer, 2011, 2016). Facilitating the accumulation of knowledge in a way that promotes the flexible, adaptive application of ID concepts is needed to help novices learn to think like an expert (Ertmer & Stepich, 2005).

This may be best accomplished by embed - ding their learning in experience. In a cross-case comparison of intro - ductory ID courses, Slagter van Tryon, McDonald, and Hirumi (2018) cite authentic experience as a key element in promoting the develop - ment of ID knowledge, skills, and dispositions. Accumulating authentic experience at multiple stages may help novices organize and contextu - alize knowledge and promote the development of ID skills and disposi - tions (Stepich & Ertmer, 2009). Second, educators should mentor and scaffold novices’ ID skills and dispositions by making their expertise and design process more explicit. Novices who receive scaffolding and guidance from skilled designers are able to more closely perform like experts (Ertmer, Stepich, et al., 2009a; Verstegen et al., 2008). Explic - itly discussing expert thinking and design decision making could help scaffold novices’ abilities.

Finally, educators can implement innovative, holistic training strategies targeting affective (i.e., dispositions), cogni - tive (i.e., knowledge), and behavioral (i.e., skills) processes. Training fostering development in these domains will promote the develop - ment of expertise. Innovative ID training and evaluation efforts would answer important and timely questions regarding how expertise devel - ops (Brown & Green, 2018).

This in-depth look at foundational scholarship, and review of current definitions, has identified a need to create a clearer conceptual definition of instructional design expertise. To do so, expert characteristics were reviewed and synthesized into overarching traits. Three primary traits (i.e., knowl - edge, skills, dispositions) emerged from this synthe - sis of expert characteristics and were used to create a new definition of instructional design expertise. This definition extends existing conceptualizations and parallels the definition of human expertise proposed by Herling (2000). Defining expertise is especially complex due to the ill-structured nature of instructional design. Compared to other disciplines where expert per - formance (e.g., chess, sports) is identified by a consistent outcome or behavior, for instructional designers, there is often not one correct path or solution.

title: Schemata, gambits and precedent: some factors in design expertise
abstract: The paper begins by outlining some methodological problems, concluding that to understand design expertise we need to recognise that such practice includes the roles of teams, communication and shared experiences and understandings. It explores the significance of experience in expertise focussing on the way precedent stored in the form of episodic schemata is used by experts to recognise design situations for which gambits are available. The paper combines evidence from new empirical data on the perception of drawings with interviews with expert designers and research on expertise from other cognitive fields. The paper concludes that design expertise cannot be understood by studying actions alone but that our research needs to concentrate on perception and recognition and that we have to examine conversations and memories as much as drawings.

title: Designing theory
abstract: Theoretical work is essential to the progress of any discipline. Theories, models, and frameworks are underdetermined representations of a phenomenon that help us understand and take action in a domain. However, the field of learning design and technology (LDT) has traditionally struggled with developing a solid theoretical foundation that is useful for both research and practice. We propose viewing theory building as an act of design might address these challenges. After defining key constructs and describing two approaches to theory development, we describe three design perspectives that might be useful for theory development: Lawson and Dorst’s (Design expertise, Elsevier, Amsterdam, 2009) view of design as a combination of analytical (problem-based) and creative (solution-based) moves, Schön’s (The reflective practitioner: how professionals think in action, Basic Books, New York, 1983) reflection-in-action, and design as dialogic interpretation (Snodgrass and Coyne in Des Issues 9(1):56–74, https://doi.org/10.2307/1511599, 1992). We use a case study to illustrate each perspective. We conclude with implications of a design approach to theory creation, including how design perspectives enable scholars to design possible futures.

In this article, we use the term design perspectives to describe ways designers and design theorists view and act in situations. We assert design perspectives provide a way to address the particular challenges of theorizing in LDT: design supports work in wicked contexts, and design couples theory and practice. First, Buchanan (1992) argued that design is particularly suited to working in wicked contexts. He defined design as a liberal art that “connect[s] and integrate[s] useful knowledge from the arts and sciences… in ways that are suited to the problems and purposes of the present” (p. 6). Goel and Pirolli (1992) also described characteristics of domains that are often approached through design rather than general problem-solving strategies.

Second, the need to tightly link theory and practice is also seen in design fields, where scholars attempt to simultaneously “embrace values of design and science” (Beck and Stolterman 2016, p. 210). As a consequence, theorizing in design research can look differ - ent from theoretical work in science-based fields. Beck and Stolterman (2016) described how design researchers often make multiple types of knowledge claims. In this section, we define models, theories, and frameworks; compare two approaches to theory development; and suggest criteria for effective theory in LDT. First, however, it is important to note that, although in this article we focus on the development of scientific theories and frameworks through design, we acknowledge that our field supports a variety of approaches and descriptions of knowledge and knowledge building. For example, professional designers have been described as having different ways of knowing and types of knowledge (Gregor and Jones 2007; Löwgren 2013) and design itself can be considered an epistemology (Lawson and Dorst 2009). For example, Elizabeth Boling has led extensive research into the importance of case-based knowledge (precedent) to the instructional design field (e.g., Boling and Gray 2018; Boling et al. 2015).

Furthermore, a “design theory” provides a different type of knowing than traditional scientific theory. Design theory moves beyond description to how to actually do something (Baskerville and Pries- Heje 2010; Gregor and Jones 2007; Lee et al. 2011). These types of theories and stores of knowledge are critical to design practice itself and should continue to be developed within the instructional design field. However, here we turn our attention to a different relationship between design and theory: we consider what design perspectives can offer the for the development of scientific theory in both instructional design and the broader LDT field.

Evidence of this can be seen through current work on technology infusion, a position that emphasizes that technology integration is the responsibility of all teacher education faculty, not a single technology instructor in a stand-alone course. In this article, we have taken a journey through theory and design in order to argue that viewing theory building from design perspectives might help the LDT field address current weaknesses: a weak theoretical foundation, and theory disconnected from practice. After explaining multiple perspectives on theory, we explored designing theory from three design perspectives: design as a combination of analytic and creative moves, design as reflection-in-action, and a hermeneutical (dialogic interpretation) approach to design. Although each perspective comes from a different philosophical orientation, each gives insight into designing theory.
